modules.intro: The order is the order of need: curves before responses, logarithms before levels, arrows before CSI, robust statistics before the instrument, counts and Bayes before the fused model, chains before dynamics.

steps.body:
A function $f$ takes an input $x$ and returns one output $y=f(x)$. You can draw it as a curve: the horizontal axis is the input, the vertical axis is the output.

In this thesis the input is usually the number of people $N$, and the output is something a radio receiver measures: a fluctuation level of the Wi-Fi channel, or a count of Bluetooth devices.

The receiver sees the output and wants $N$. So the thesis asks a reverse question: given the output, what was the input? That reverse question is only easy where the curve is steep.
implies: Every observation model in the thesis has this shape: an input you want, an output you measure.
Going backwards, from output to input, is the whole problem of counting.

symbols.meaning: the input (later: the count of people $N$)
the rule that turns the input into the output
the output (later: a measured level or device count)

steps.title: A function is a rule from input to output

steps.body:
The slope at a point says how much $y$ changes when $x$ changes a little. For a curve, the slope at $x$ is the derivative $f'(x)$.

Turn this around. If the measurement of $y$ has an error of size $\sigma$, the error it causes in the recovered $x$ is about $\sigma/|f'(x)|$. A steep curve turns a small output error into a small input error. A flat curve turns the same output error into a large input error.

check.answer: About $0.1/0.5=0.2$ at $x=1$ and $0.1/0.05=2$ at $x=6$. The same measurement is ten times less informative where the curve is ten times flatter.
check.question: A curve has slope 0.5 at $x=1$ and slope 0.05 at $x=6$. The output error is 0.1 at both points. What input error do you get at each point?

implies: Where the response is flat, no amount of careful measurement of the output pins down the input.
Count resolution is a property of the curve at the current count, not one number for the whole system.

symbols.meaning: a small step in the input
an error or uncertainty in the measured output
the error it causes in the recovered input

steps.title: The slope is the exchange rate between input and output

steps.body:
The function $\log(1+x/s)$ starts at 0, rises steeply, and keeps growing ever more slowly. At $x=s$ it has reached $\log 2$. The number $s$ is the "half-saturation" scale: below it the curve is nearly a straight line, above it the curve flattens.

The thesis models the CSI fluctuation level as a saturating function of the number of people: the first people change the channel a lot, the hundredth person changes it a little (Module 3). The widget shows the related curve $1-e^{-x/K}$, which has the same shape.
implies: A saturating response is informative at small counts and nearly blind at large ones.
Stretching $x$ and $s$ by the same factor leaves the curve unchanged. That stretch is the scale problem of Module 3.

symbols.meaning: the half-saturation scale, in the unit of $x$
the slope, which falls as $x$ grows

steps.title: Saturating curves

lessons.summary: A function maps an input to an output. Its slope says how much the output moves per unit of input, and that one number decides how well an output can tell you the input.
lessons.thesis: Used in the fused model (Module 3) and in the outputs (Module 4)
lessons.title: Functions, slopes and saturation

steps.body:
$\ln x$ is the power you must raise $e\approx2.718$ to in order to get $x$. Its key property: $\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b$. So a ratio $a/b$ becomes a difference $\ln a-\ln b$.

The thesis measures how strongly the Wi-Fi channel fluctuates and takes the logarithm of that spread. A receiver whose gain is twice as high has every spread twice as large, which adds the same constant $\ln 2\approx0.69$ to every logarithm. Subtracting a reference level removes that constant. That is why the instrument works in log units (Module 2).
implies: A constant gain factor becomes a constant offset, which a reference level removes.
One unit of $\ln$ is a factor of $e\approx2.7$; 1.7 units, the busy-day response of Module 2, is a factor of about 5.5.

symbols.meaning: two positive numbers, for example two spreads

steps.title: The logarithm turns ratios into differences

steps.body:
Radio engineers write power ratios in decibels: $10\log_{10}(P/P_0)$. A factor of 10 in power is 10 dB, a factor of 2 is about 3 dB. Amplitude is the square root of power, so an amplitude ratio $a/a_0$ is $20\log_{10}(a/a_0)$ dB.

The fleet stores CSI amplitudes and their ratios in dB. The fluctuation level of Module 2 is the logarithm of a spread measured in dB.
implies: Decibels and natural logarithms are the same idea with different bases.

symbols.meaning: a power and a reference power
an amplitude and a reference amplitude

steps.title: Decibels are the engineer's logarithm

lessons.summary: A logarithm turns multiplication into addition, so ratios become differences.
lessons.thesis: Used for the CSI level (Module 2) and the amplitude in decibels (Module 1)
lessons.title: Logarithms and decibels

steps.body:
A pure wave is $a\cos(2\pi f t+\varphi)$. The amplitude $a$ is its height, the frequency $f$ is how many cycles it makes per second, and the phase $\varphi$ is where in its cycle it starts.

The thesis fleet works on Wi-Fi channel 48 at 5,240 MHz: 5.24 billion cycles per second. The wavelength is $\lambda=c/f\approx 5.7$ cm.
implies: At 5 GHz a body that moves a few centimetres changes a path by a large fraction of a wavelength.
steps.title: A wave has an amplitude, a frequency and a phase

steps.body:
A copy of the wave that arrives $\tau$ seconds later is $a\cos(2\pi f(t-\tau))$: the delay looks like a phase shift of $-2\pi f\tau$.

The same delay rotates the phase by a different angle at each frequency. Wi-Fi sends many frequencies at once (subcarriers), so one path delay shows up as a phase that changes steadily across the subcarriers.
implies: A path length change of one wavelength turns the phase once.

symbols.meaning: delay of the copy, in seconds
the phase shift the delay causes, in radians

steps.title: A delay is a phase shift that grows with frequency

lessons.summary: A radio signal is a wave. A delay shifts its phase by an angle proportional to the frequency, which is why one path looks different on each subcarrier.
lessons.title: Waves, phase and delay

steps.body:
A wave of amplitude $a$ and phase $\varphi$ can be stored as one complex number $z=ae^{j\varphi}$: an arrow of length $a$ at angle $\varphi$. Engineers write $j$ for the imaginary unit, $j^2=-1$.

CSI is a table of such arrows: one per subcarrier and antenna pair, refreshed with every received frame.
implies: Amplitude keeps the length and throws away the angle.
steps.title: A complex number is a length and an angle

steps.body:
Multiplying two arrows multiplies their lengths and adds their angles. Dividing divides the lengths and subtracts the angles.

So a receiver error that multiplies every value by the same unknown factor $g e^{j\phi}$ cancels when you divide two values that both carry it. The fleet uses the ratio of two receive chains for exactly this reason (Module 1).
implies: A shared multiplicative disturbance cancels in a ratio, and only a shared one does.
steps.title: Multiplying turns and stretches, dividing cancels

steps.body:
Two copies of a wave that arrive together add as arrows, head to tail. Pointing the same way, they reinforce. Pointing opposite ways, they cancel.

The squared length of the sum has a cross term that depends on the angle between the arrows. A small movement changes that angle, so the sum flickers. That is why moving people make CSI fluctuate.
implies: Fluctuation, not the average level, carries the information about moving bodies.
steps.title: Adding arrows is interference

lessons.summary: A complex number is an arrow with a length and an angle. Multiplying turns and stretches it, dividing undoes that, adding arrows gives interference.
lessons.title: Complex numbers as arrows

steps.body:
Take $m$ samples $x_1,\dots,x_m$ from a short window. Their mean $\bar x$ is the sum divided by $m$. The standard deviation $s$ measures the typical distance from the mean.

The fleet computes one such spread for every 2-second window of CSI from the illuminating transmitter. A quiet room gives a small spread, a room with moving people a large one.
implies: One spread per window turns a fast, noisy signal into a slow summary of how busy the channel is.

symbols.meaning: number of samples in the window

steps.title: The standard deviation measures how much values wander

steps.body:
The median is the middle value after sorting. If one value out of nine is wildly wrong, the mean moves with it, but the median barely moves.

The median absolute deviation (MAD) is the median distance from the median. Multiplied by 1.4826, it estimates the standard deviation of normally distributed data, yet it ignores outliers.

The thesis uses medians twice. The level of one receiver is the median over a minute of log spreads. The panel level is the median across receivers, which is why one receiver that misbehaves does not move it (Module 2).

check.answer: The mean is about 0.23, pulled up by the 1.9. The median is 0.1. The one wild receiver moves the median by at most one rank.
check.question: Nine receivers read 0.1, 0.0, −0.2, 0.1, 0.0, 0.2, −0.1, 0.1 and 1.9. What are the mean and the median?

implies: A median across several sensors is robust to one sensor that drifts or fails.
steps.title: The median ignores a few wild values

lessons.summary: The standard deviation measures how much values wander. The median and the median absolute deviation do the same job while ignoring a few wild values.
lessons.thesis: Used for the CSI level and the panel floor (Module 2)
lessons.title: Spread, median and robust summaries

steps.body:
A count of detected devices is a whole number: 0, 1, 2, and so on. The Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda$ is the simplest model for counts. Its variance equals its mean.

Real device counts often vary more than that, because people carry different numbers of devices. The negative binomial adds a shape parameter $r$: its variance is $\mu+\mu^2/r$. A large $r$ brings it back to the Poisson.
implies: Overdispersion is the statistical signature of people who carry different numbers of devices.

symbols.meaning: a count, for example detected Bluetooth devices
one possible value of that count
shape of the negative binomial (large $r$: close to Poisson)

steps.title: Distributions for counts: Poisson and negative binomial

steps.body:
A likelihood $p(y\mid N=k)$ says how probable the observation $y$ is if the count were $k$. Bayes' rule reverses the direction: the probability of each count after the observation is proportional to the likelihood times the prior probability of that count.

The prior includes the list of counts that are allowed at all, the support $\{0,\dots,N_{\max}\}$. In the thesis that list ends at a capacity bound derived from the surveyed seats.
implies: When the likelihood is flat over many counts, the prior decides. A confident posterior is then a statement about the prior, not about the data.

symbols.meaning: likelihood: how probable the observation is if the count were $k$
prior: the probability of count $k$ before the observation
the largest count the model allows (the support)
posterior: the probability of count $k$ after the observation

steps.title: Bayes' rule turns a likelihood into a distribution over the count

lessons.summary: The Poisson and negative binomial distributions describe counts. Bayes' rule turns the probability of an observation into a probability over the unknown count.
lessons.title: Count distributions and Bayes' rule

steps.body:
A Markov chain has states, here the possible counts $0,\dots,N_{\max}$, and a transition matrix $T$. The entry $T_{nm}$ is the probability of moving from count $n$ now to count $m$ one minute later. Each row sums to one.

If $p_t$ is the probability over counts at minute $t$, the probability one minute later is $p_t T$: a row vector times the matrix.
implies: Occupancy changes slowly, so most of the probability stays near the current count. That is what lets a filter accumulate weak evidence over time.

symbols.meaning: the probabilities of all counts at minute $t$

steps.title: A Markov chain forgets everything but the present

steps.body:
A filter keeps a belief $b_t$ over counts. Each minute it does two things.

1. **Predict:** move the belief through the chain, $b_t T$. The belief spreads a little, because people arrive and leave.
2. **Correct:** multiply by the likelihood of the new observation and renormalise. This is Bayes' rule.

A filtered belief uses only the past and the present, which is what a deployed estimator has.
implies: Several weak sensors combine by multiplying their likelihoods inside the correction step.

symbols.meaning: the belief that the count is $n$ at minute $t$
the observations of the next minute

steps.title: A filter alternates prediction and correction

lessons.summary: A Markov chain moves between states with probabilities that depend only on the current state. A filter runs Bayes' rule through such a chain, one time step after another.
lessons.title: Markov chains

modules.subtitle: The mathematics the thesis assumes, from school level
modules.title: Foundations

modules.intro: The module covers the question, the hypotheses, and the two kinds of radio evidence the estimator fuses: device-free CSI, which responds to bodies, and device-based Bluetooth, which counts phones and laptops.

steps.body:
The target is the number of people $N_t$ in the library (open area and silent room together) during minute $t$. The estimator does not output one number. It outputs a probability for every possible count, and from that two simpler readouts:

- **levels:** empty (0), low (1–30), busy (31 or more);
- **count bands:** 0 · 1–10 · 11–30 · 31–60 · 61–100 · 101+, each with a probability, and the smallest set of bands that holds 90 % of it.

Manual counts are never an input. They are taken only to check frozen predictions.
implies: A level or a band is a sum of these probabilities over a range of counts.
Missing data is "no answer", never "zero people".
steps.latex: p_t(k)=P(N_t=k\mid\text{CSI and BLE observations up to minute }t)

symbols.meaning: the number of people in the library during minute $t$
one possible value of that number
the probability the estimator assigns to "$k$ people"

steps.title: The answer is a probability over counts

steps.body:
- **H1 (instrument).** Single receivers drift between empty nights, but the median across receivers varies less than the difference between an empty and a busy library.
- **H2 (levels).** Fusing Wi-Fi CSI, Bluetooth and ambient Wi-Fi classifies empty / low / busy on blind dates better than a time-of-day guess and better than each sensor alone.
- **H3 (bands).** With the person scale taken only from declared outside information, the 90 % band sets contain the true count about 90 % of the time on blind dates, while staying narrower than "anything is possible".

H1 is a property of the measuring instrument (Module 2). H2 and H3 are properties of the fused model (Modules 3 and 4), scored against counts taken 20–31 October 2026.
steps.title: Three hypotheses

steps.body:
Column 1 is the key to this thesis. Either the body changes a radio link (device-free: CSI, RSSI, radar) or a carried device transmits (Bluetooth, Wi-Fi management frames). The first has no person scale; the second counts devices, not people.

The estimator uses one of each. Each fails where the other helps: CSI sees people without phones, Bluetooth gives a number.

figure.caption: Comparison begins with the observation mechanism, then the target and deployment shift. The taxonomy separates device emissions from body-sensitive propagation and is synthesised from the cited modality and CSI literature.

steps.title: Two ways a person enters a radio measurement

lessons.summary: The thesis estimates how many people are in a public library from two cheap radio signals, without ever training on manual counts, and then checks its answers and their stated confidence on days it has never seen.
lessons.title: The question and the plan

steps.body:
Wi-Fi splits one channel into many narrow subcarriers. On subcarrier $k$ the transmitter sends a known training symbol $X_k$. What arrives is $Y_k$: the symbol multiplied by the channel $H_k$, plus noise.

Because $X_k$ is known, the receiver can estimate $H_k\approx Y_k/X_k$. That estimate, a complex number per subcarrier and antenna pair, refreshed with every frame, is the Channel State Information.

In the thesis fleet the receivers are Intel AX210 cards on channel 48 (5,240 MHz, 20 MHz wide), with 52 tones per receive chain.
implies: CSI measures a propagation channel, not people.

symbols.meaning: subcarrier index (one narrow frequency inside the Wi-Fi channel)
the known training symbol sent on subcarrier $k$
what the receiver observed on subcarrier $k$
the complex channel coefficient: how the room changed the symbol

steps.title: The receiver estimates the channel from known symbols

steps.body:
The signal reaches the receiver along several paths: straight across, off a wall, off a shelf, off a person. Path $p$ has a complex coefficient $a_p$ and a delay $\tau_p$.

At subcarrier frequency $f_k$, the delay rotates path $p$ by the angle $2\pi f_k\tau_p$ (Module 0). The channel is the sum of these rotated arrows. A moving body changes its own path and can block others, so the sum fluctuates. An empty room gives a still pattern; a busy room gives a flickering one.
implies: A change says that some path changed. It does not say how many bodies changed it.

symbols.meaning: complex coefficient of path $p$: its strength and phase

steps.title: The channel is a sum of paths

steps.body: The left box is the room: static paths and one body-sensitive path. The middle box is the path sum. The right box is the instrument: gain, phase and timing effects act before CSI is stored. The stored value carries a tilde, $\widetilde H$, because it is not the true channel.

figure.caption: CSI is a superposition of propagation paths observed through an imperfect instrument. The schematic separates body-sensitive propagation from hardware and acquisition effects; it is not a surveyed ray trace.

steps.title: Propagation, then instrument

steps.body:
The receiver stores the true channel multiplied by an amplitude scale $g_r$ and a phase rotation, plus noise. The phase rotation has a part common to every subcarrier, a part that grows with the subcarrier index (timing), and a fixed offset per receive chain.

This explains why raw CSI phase looks random from frame to frame, and why amplitude can jump when the automatic gain control steps.
implies: A raw amplitude level mixes people with receiver gain. The instrument must remove the gain before it reads people.
steps.title: What the receiver actually stores

steps.body:
Divide two receive chains at the same subcarrier and frame. Every factor they share cancels (Module 0): the common phase, the timing slope, and the time variation of the gain. What remains is the difference between how the room affects the two antennas.

The fleet's CSI feature starts from this chain ratio, in dB. Its fluctuation over 2-second windows is the raw material of the instrument level in Module 2.
implies: A ratio helps only against disturbances both chains share.
steps.title: Dividing two chains cancels what they share

steps.body:
In (a), late in the evening, the stripes stay still: the static paths make a fixed pattern. In (b), during a busy evening hour, the pattern flickers as paths change.

Panel (c) reduces each 2-s window to one number, its spread, on a log axis. The busy windows sit far above the quiet ones. Module 2 turns exactly this spread into the instrument level.

figure.caption: Receiver monad04, illuminator monad01, channel 48 (5,240 MHz, HT20), 52 tones, chain rx0, 28 September 2026. (a), (b): 30 s of amplitude per subcarrier on a shared colour scale. (c): amplitude standard deviation per 2-s window over 10 min around each interval. The figure illustrates the observable; it is not a count result.

steps.title: Real CSI on one fleet link, quiet and busy

lessons.summary: Wi-Fi sends known symbols on many subcarriers. The receiver divides what arrived by what was sent and gets one complex channel coefficient per subcarrier, which is a sum of propagation paths.
lessons.thesis: Foundations and Related Work; The Instrument
lessons.title: What CSI measures

steps.body:
A Bluetooth Low Energy device sends short advertisements, typically several per second. Each carries an address. Static devices in the building use fixed public addresses; personal devices use random addresses that rotate for privacy. On the fleet, non-resolvable addresses rotate on a 10-minute clock and resolvable ones within about 15 minutes (measured 27 September).

Every fleet node listens continuously. It never stores raw addresses: it stores a salted hash, so a device can be counted but not identified. Since 24 September nine nodes share one salt per half-hour, so a hash heard by two nodes is the same device.
implies: Public addresses are the empty building's background and are removed before counting.
A rotating address can make one device look like two over a long window; within one minute this effect is small.
steps.title: Devices announce themselves, under changing names

steps.body:
Each node hears only part of the room, and one device is heard by several nodes: on weekdays 4.4–5.5 of the nine. Adding the nodes' counts would count one phone five times. The fleet therefore takes the union of distinct hashes across nodes, per minute.

The estimator keeps only devices heard at −70 dBm or stronger at some node, a spatial filter that favours devices inside the library. On weekdays this keeps 64–70 % of the union.
implies: The union removes double counting across nodes; it does not turn devices into people.

symbols.meaning: the room-level Bluetooth count of minute $t$
the non-public device hashes heard by node $j$ in minute $t$, keeping only devices whose best signal at some node is $-70$ dBm or stronger
union: a device heard by several nodes appears once

steps.title: The room count is a union over nodes

steps.body:
Read panel (a) from the bottom up. At 14:00 the median node hears about 178 devices a minute. The union over all nodes reaches about 327, because each node hears devices the others miss, yet each device is counted once although four to five nodes hear it. The near union, about 223 at the same hour, keeps the devices that are close to some node.

The dashed line is the number of seats. It is in people, the curves are in devices: the gap between them is the devices-per-person scale of Module 3.

Panel (b) shows that the mix is stable from day to day: about 70 % Apple, 11–14 % Microsoft, 12–16 % without a vendor id, no Google.

figure.caption: The Bluetooth room count is a union over nine nodes. (a) Monday 5 October 2026, 06:00–22:00, hourly means of per-minute values: union of distinct non-public devices over all nine fleet-salt nodes (grey), the near union at −70 dBm or stronger that the estimator uses (blue), and the median count of a single node (dotted). The dashed line marks the 107 surveyed seats, which count people, not devices. (b) Share of union devices by Bluetooth company id, one dot per Monday-to-Thursday weekday 28 Sep – 8 Oct, 10:00–16:00; the bar is the median.

steps.title: The room count on one weekday

steps.body:
On eight Monday-to-Thursday weekdays between 28 September and 8 October, 10:00–16:00, 69–73 % of the heard non-public devices are Apple, 11–14 % Microsoft (Windows laptops), 12–16 % carry no vendor id, and Google is absent: idle Android phones mostly do not advertise.

On Monday 5 October at 14:00 the fleet heard about 327 distinct devices a minute, while the library has 107 surveyed seats. So a person carries more than one advertising device on average, or devices outside the library are heard, or both. Weekend middays read 4–12 devices.

The number of devices per person is the missing scale. No published study gives it for Bluetooth; Module 3 shows how the thesis handles it.
implies: Bluetooth gives a number, but in units of devices.
CSI gives a response to bodies, but with no unit at all.
steps.title: Who is heard, and why devices are not people

lessons.summary: Phones, laptops and watches broadcast short Bluetooth messages with rotating addresses. The fleet counts distinct devices per minute across all nodes. The count is about devices, not people.
lessons.thesis: Foundations and Related Work; The Library Corpus
lessons.title: What Bluetooth counts

modules.subtitle: What the thesis asks, what Wi-Fi CSI measures, and what Bluetooth counts
modules.title: Two kinds of radio evidence

modules.intro: The module builds the instrument's CSI level from the raw channel, defines when the library counts as certifiably empty, and assesses H1: single receivers drift, the panel does not.

steps.body:
The open area (343.9 m²) holds the illuminator monad01 near its centre and seven receivers; two more receivers (monad07, monad09) sit in the silent room (69.8 m²) behind a wall. Each line is one link.

The library has 107 surveyed seats in the two rooms. The estimator's count grid ends at 160, to leave room for people standing.

figure.caption: Fleet layout in the FIIT library, from the surveyed floor plan. monad01 illuminates (TX) and the nine other nodes observe (RX). Lines mark TX–RX link pairs, not propagation paths. All nodes stand 0.9 m above the floor.

steps.title: Ten nodes, one illuminator

steps.body:
CSI exists only for frames the receiver hears. Ambient Wi-Fi traffic comes and goes with users, so its frames arrive irregularly. The AX210 cannot run as a 5 GHz access point, so the fleet makes its own traffic: monad01 sends short frames at a fixed pace, 250 per second on channel 48, in monitor mode.

Every receiver keeps only the frames from that one transmitter for the CSI level. That makes the measurement regular: the same transmitter, the same rate, all day.
implies: The transmitter's own counter counts frames handed to the driver, not frames on air; delivery is measured at the receivers.
steps.title: Paced illumination instead of an access point

lessons.summary: Ten Raspberry Pi 5 nodes with Intel AX210 cards measure the library. One node transmits paced frames; nine record them and listen to Bluetooth.
lessons.title: The fleet and its illumination

steps.body:
Take the chain-ratio amplitude in dB of the illuminator's frames (Module 1). In each 2-second window $w$, compute its standard deviation $s_w$ (Module 0). Take the logarithm, because a gain change then becomes an offset. The level of receiver $j$ in minute $t$ is the median of these log spreads over the minute's windows.

This statistic comes from the lake's 2-second table. On 5 October it reproduces an earlier packet-by-packet computation at Pearson 0.986–0.998 on all nine receivers.
implies: More movement in the room means larger spreads and a higher level.
A constant gain difference between receivers becomes a constant offset in $L$.

symbols.meaning: spread (SD, dB) of receiver $j$ in 2-second window $w$
level of receiver $j$ in minute $t$, in ln units

steps.title: The receiver level

steps.body:
A level means nothing until it is compared with the same receiver in an empty library. That reference is the floor $F_j$.

"Empty" needs two independent conditions together:

1. the library is closed (it is open every day 06:00–22:00);
2. the Bluetooth room count sits at its night floor.

A closed schedule alone is not enough: cleaners and late readers exist. On the nine development nights 11,012 of 11,064 closed receiver-minutes (99.5 %) also passed the Bluetooth condition, a median of 123 certified minutes per receiver and night.
implies: A Bluetooth count of zero does not exclude a person without an advertising device. "Certified empty" is a declared rule, not a proof.

symbols.meaning: the floor of receiver $j$ (median level on certified-empty minutes)
the certified-empty minutes: library closed and $B_t$ at or below the night floor

steps.title: The floor is the level of an empty library

lessons.summary: Each 2-second window of chain-ratio amplitude gives one spread. The median of the log spreads over a minute is the receiver's level.
lessons.thesis: The Instrument; A Fused Occupancy Estimator
lessons.title: From frames to one level per receiver and minute

steps.body:
Compute one floor per receiver per night instead of one for all nights, relative to that receiver's floor over all nights. On the development nights single receivers jump by 1–2 ln units: monad09 reads +1.83 on the night of 6 October against −0.25 to +0.18 on its other nights; monad05 reads +2.25 on 30 September against −0.84 to +0.95 later.

The jumps hit one receiver at a time, on the same transmitter, channel and rate as every other night. The cause is open.
implies: A model that trusts one receiver's floor would read phantom people on some nights.
steps.title: Single receivers drift between empty nights

steps.body:
At each minute, take the level above the floor of every receiver that reports, and keep the median. With nine receivers, one that jumps moves the median by at most one rank (Module 0). That is the panel level $P_t$.

The same idea gives one panel floor per night: the median across receivers of each receiver's certified-empty level on that night, relative to its own reference floor.
implies: Redundancy across links, not the stability of any one link, makes the instrument usable.

symbols.meaning: the panel level of minute $t$ (at least 4 receivers)

steps.title: The panel is the median across receivers

steps.body:
H1 compares two quantities in the same unit:

- how much the panel floor wanders between empty nights: the standard deviation of $\Phi_n$ over nights;
- how much a busy day lifts the panel: the median over weekdays of the panel level between 10:00 and 16:00.

H1 passes if their ratio is at most 0.5, a threshold fixed before the computation. At 0.5 the busy level sits two night-to-night standard deviations above the floor.

On the nine development nights: panel floor SD 0.179 ln; busy response 1.741 ln (six weekdays, 1.41–1.97); **ratio 0.103**, with a resampling range over nights of 0.049–0.135. Single receivers give 0.20–0.55; monad05 alone would fail at 0.55.

check.answer: Its ratio is $0.6/1.7\approx0.35$, below 0.5, so yes, but far less comfortably than the panel at 0.103. monad05 at SD 0.96 gives 0.55 and fails.
check.question: A single receiver has floor SD 0.6 ln and the same busy response 1.7 ln. Does it pass the declared threshold on its own?

implies: The median across links cuts the night-to-night spread by a factor of about 2–5 compared with single links (single-receiver SD 0.35–0.96 ln).

symbols.meaning: the H1 ratio (pass if at most 0.5)

steps.title: The H1 ratio

steps.body:
Every grey line is one receiver. Two of them jump into the busy band on a night when the library was empty: monad05 on 30 September and monad09 on 6 October. Others reach above 1 ln. A model that trusted any single receiver would read a full library on some nights.

The blue line is the median across receivers. It stays between −0.37 and +0.26 ln on every night, far below the shaded busy band. Its spread over nights, 0.179 ln, divided by the busy response, 1.74 ln, is the H1 ratio 0.103.

figure.caption: Single receivers drift between certified-empty nights; the nine-link median does not. Grey: each receiver's median level over certified-empty minutes of one night, relative to that receiver's reference floor (nine development nights 30 Sep – 8 Oct 2026, each with at least six receivers; certified minutes from the reference night, empty night and early-morning drift captures of the same transmitter, channel and rate). A line breaks where a receiver has no certified minutes. Blue: the panel floor, the median across receivers. Shaded band: the weekday busy response of the panel, median 1.74 ln, range over six weekdays 1.41–1.97.

steps.title: The drift and the panel in one picture

steps.body:
The result is preliminary. It rests on nine nights, with a median of about two hours of certified minutes per receiver and night, and the busy window is only partly sampled, because the afternoon captures start after 12:00. It uses development days.

The month assessment uses 12–31 October. The calendar to 19 October gives every night from 11 to 18 October a capture of the same configuration from 04:00 until opening, and every night except 12 October also one from 22:00 (until 03:30 on 13 and 14 October). The single-receiver drift is reported alongside the ratio as part of the instrument characterisation, together with delivery, timing and receiver effects.
implies: Characterisation is not counting accuracy. H1 says the instrument can see the difference between empty and busy, not how many people are there.
steps.title: What this result does not yet say

lessons.summary: One receiver's empty floor jumps from night to night. The median across receivers barely moves, compared with how much a busy day lifts it.
lessons.title: H1 — single links drift, the panel does not

modules.subtitle: Ten radios, one illuminator, and why the median across links is steady (H1)
modules.title: The instrument

modules.intro: The estimator treats the number of people as a hidden quantity that changes slowly. The Bluetooth count and the CSI panel level are two noisy witnesses of it. One number, devices per person, cannot be learned from the radio data; the model carries it as a declared range.

steps.body:
Each minute, each person present stays with probability $1-\mu$, and a random number of new people arrive. The number who stay is binomial; the number who arrive is Poisson with mean $\lambda_t$.

This is the immigration–death process. It gives the transition matrix $T$ of Module 0, one for each arrival rate. If the arrival rate stayed fixed, the count would settle around $\lambda/\mu$ people.
implies: With $\mu=1/90$ (the selected value), a person stays 90 minutes on average.
Many people can arrive or leave in one minute, as at the start of a lecture break.

symbols.meaning: probability that a person leaves in one minute

steps.title: Arrivals and departures

steps.body:
The arrival rate depends on the day class (Monday–Thursday, Friday, weekend) and the hour: $\lambda_{c,h}$. It is learned from unlabelled radio data, not from counts.

Run with no observations at all, the chain alone produces the calendar guess: "a Monday at 14:00 is usually like this". That calendar-only prediction is the first comparator for H2.
implies: Fridays carry far fewer devices than other weekdays, so they get their own rates.
steps.title: The calendar lives in the arrival rate

lessons.summary: People arrive at a rate that depends on the day and the hour, and each person leaves with a small probability every minute. That gives a Markov chain over counts.
lessons.title: The hidden count and how it moves

steps.body:
The Bluetooth room count $B_t$ (Module 1) is a background plus a contribution from the people present. Each person contributes a random number of heard devices with mean $\alpha$, so $N$ people contribute on average $\alpha N$. Because people differ, the total varies more than a Poisson count: a negative binomial whose shape grows with $N$.

The background $b_0$ comes from the empty night. The shape per person $k$ was selected from the data (Module 3, last lesson).
implies: Bluetooth constrains $\alpha N$, the number of devices, not $N$ itself.

symbols.meaning: mean and shape of the empty-library background
devices heard per person: the unknown scale

steps.title: The Bluetooth witness

steps.body:
The CSI panel level $P_t$ (Module 2) rises with the number of people and flattens as the room fills (Module 0, saturation). Its noise is mostly Gaussian, but some minutes are off for reasons other than people. A 10 % wide component, four times as broad, keeps such a minute from producing a confidently wrong count.

The intercept, slope, half-saturation and width are learned from unlabelled data, jointly with Bluetooth. So CSI takes its person scale from Bluetooth through the fit; it has no scale of its own.
implies: CSI fills the gaps Bluetooth leaves: people without advertising devices, and fast changes within the hour.

symbols.meaning: intercept, slope and half-saturation of the CSI response

steps.title: The CSI witness

steps.body:
Each minute the filter predicts with the chain, then multiplies by both likelihoods and renormalises (Module 0). Multiplying likelihoods is how independent evidence combines: a count that both witnesses find plausible gains weight, a count either one finds implausible loses it.

A missing witness simply contributes nothing that minute. The filter keeps running on the other.
implies: Other sensors (CO₂, radar, round-trip time) would enter as further likelihood factors, each with its own scale and delay.

symbols.meaning: the belief that $m$ people are present at minute $t$
the transition matrix with the arrival rate of minute $t$

steps.title: The witnesses meet in the filter

lessons.summary: The Bluetooth count is a negative binomial whose mean grows with the number of people. The CSI panel level is a saturating curve of the number of people, with an allowance for odd minutes.
lessons.title: Two witnesses

steps.body:
Suppose the true situation is $N$ people with $\alpha$ devices each. Now imagine $2N$ people with $\alpha/2$ devices each, arriving twice as fast, with the CSI curve stretched twice as wide. Bluetooth sees the same $\alpha N$ devices. CSI sees the same level. Nothing in the radio data tells the two worlds apart, apart from small effects of counting noise and of the capacity bound.

This is the global-gain ambiguity known from blind sensor calibration. Radio data alone cannot fix it reliably. Only outside information about the scale can.
implies: Counting devices well is not counting people well.
steps.latex: (N,\ \lambda,\ s,\ \alpha,\ k)\ \longrightarrow\ (cN,\ c\lambda,\ cs,\ \alpha/c,\ k/c)\quad\text{leaves}\ \ \alpha N,\ \ kN\ \ \text{and}\ \ \tfrac{N}{s}\ \ \text{unchanged}
steps.title: Twice the people, half the devices each

steps.body:
The corpus and a web search found no measurement of Bluetooth devices per person. The thesis therefore declares a range from outside facts: an iPhone advertises while Bluetooth is on, laptops and watches add devices, idle Android phones mostly do not, and some heard devices are outside the library.

- **Prior A (primary):** log-normal, median 2 devices per person, geometric SD 2 (central 95 %: 0.5 to 8).
- **Prior B (check):** log-uniform from 0.7 to 6.

Both are fixed before any count is opened, and both are scored. The capacity bound (count grid up to 160) and the certified-empty zero are the other two pieces of outside information.
implies: If the prior is wrong, the 90 % bands will miss on the blind dates. That is the test of H3, not a flaw to repair with counts.
steps.title: A declared range for devices per person

steps.body:
The model runs one filter for each of seven values of $\alpha$ spread over the prior, and mixes their answers with the prior weights. A small $\alpha$ means many people per device; a large $\alpha$ means few.

Letting the data reweight the seven values (by how well each explains the radio data) collapsed onto a single value, $\alpha\approx4.5$, on the development days. That collapse follows the model's assumptions about arrival noise, not real scale information, so it is kept only as an exploratory variant.
implies: The output is wide where the scale matters and narrow where it does not: empty versus occupied needs no scale at all.

symbols.meaning: the seven scale values and their prior weights

steps.title: Carrying the scale through every answer

lessons.summary: Doubling the number of people while halving the devices per person leaves every observation unchanged. The thesis states a range for devices per person from outside information and carries that uncertainty into every output.
lessons.title: The scale nobody can learn from the radio

steps.body:
Start from a rough model. Run the filter forwards and backwards over the training days to get the most plausible count for every minute. Then update the arrival rates from the implied arrivals, and refit the CSI curve by weighted least squares. Repeat a few times.

No count, survey or app record enters this loop. The training days are 25 September – 8 October for Bluetooth and from 30 September for CSI.
implies: The fit learns how the witnesses relate to each other and to the calendar; it cannot learn the scale.
steps.title: Expectation-maximisation from unlabelled days

steps.body:
Each held-out day from 2 to 8 October was predicted from the days before it. The score was how well the model predicted the next minute's Bluetooth count: a label-free criterion.

Selected by the declared rules: the near-filtered Bluetooth count, departure probability $\mu=1/90$, shape per person $k=8$, CSI panel level with the 10 % wide component, fixed receiver floors. Ambient Wi-Fi rate and cross-receiver dispersion lost on a 5 October day and were dropped. Re-zeroing the floors each day lost on 7 October and was not adopted.

Does CSI add anything? A filter that sees only CSI predicted the next Bluetooth count better than the calendar alone on four of six days (+0.14 to +2.33 nats per minute) and worse on two (−0.03 and −1.47). A modest signal beyond the clock, varying from day to day.
implies: Selecting on Bluetooth prediction selects for tracking devices. The person scale is never selected on data.
The selection is re-run on 13–17 October data before the freeze on 18 October.
steps.title: What was selected, and why

lessons.summary: The arrival rates and the CSI curve are learned by expectation-maximisation from unlabelled days. Variants are chosen by rules written down before their scores were read.
lessons.title: Learning without labels, choosing by declared rules

modules.subtitle: A hidden count, two noisy witnesses, and an honest unknown scale
modules.title: The fused model

steps.body:
The posterior $p_t(k)$ gives a probability for every count. A band is a range of counts, so its probability is the sum over that range. The thesis bands are 0 · 1–10 · 11–30 · 31–60 · 61–100 · 101+. The levels are coarser bands: empty (0), low (1–30), busy (31+).

The band edges were chosen by the researcher from the room (107 seats), before any count was opened. They are narrow where counting by eye is exact and wide where it is hard.
implies: Empty versus occupied is the band [0,1) against the rest. It needs no person scale: no people means no devices beyond the background and a CSI level at the floor.

symbols.meaning: the counts from $a$ up to, but not including, $b$

steps.title: Bands and levels are sums over counts

steps.body:
Sort the bands by probability, highest first, and keep adding bands until their total reaches 90 %. That set is the stated answer: "90 % sure it is 31–60 or 61–100".

A set that spans many bands is an honest "I cannot tell more precisely". The estimator always answers; it never withholds a minute. An always-wide answer cannot win, because width is scored too.
implies: Coverage without width is cheap: the set of all bands always covers.
steps.latex: S_t=\text{smallest set of bands with}\ \sum_{b\in S_t}P_t(b)\ge0.9
steps.title: The 90 % band set

steps.body:
A rehearsal of the freeze was fitted on 25 September – 8 October and run on 8 October, a development day, not a test.

- At night, P(empty) is 0.99–1.00.
- At the weekday peak, the posterior mean under priors A and B is 110–116 people, near the 107-seat capacity.
- The 90 % sets span about 3 of the 6 bands.

The width is the price of the unknown devices-per-person scale. The variant that lets the data reweight the scale reads about 58 people with near-certain single bands: overconfident, which is why it is exploratory only.
implies: A wide answer is not a failure if it is right 90 % of the time. Whether it is, the counts will show.
steps.title: What the outputs look like (a development day)

lessons.summary: Levels and bands are sums of the posterior over ranges of counts. The 90 % band set is the smallest set of bands that holds 90 % of the probability.
lessons.thesis: A Fused Occupancy Estimator; Blind Evaluation
lessons.title: From a probability over counts to readable answers

steps.body:
For ordered outcomes, compare the predicted cumulative probability with the observed one, band by band, and add the squared differences. A forecast that put all probability on the true band scores 0. Probability on a neighbouring band costs less than probability far away.

The score is proper: a forecaster minimises the expected score only by reporting what they actually believe. H2 compares this score for the fused model against the calendar-only model and each single sensor, per counted date.
implies: A confident wrong forecast scores worse than an honest wide one.

symbols.meaning: number of ordered bands (3 for levels, 6 for count bands)

steps.title: The ranked probability score

steps.body:
Coverage is the fraction of counted sweeps whose true band lies inside the 90 % set. H3 asks whether it is close to 0.90, within a tolerance fixed before the counts are opened. Width is the number of bands in the set; it must stay below the "all bands" answer.

Both priors, A and B, are scored. Which one holds coverage tells what outside scale information is enough.
implies: Coverage far below 0.90 means the scale prior or the model is too confident. Coverage near 1 with very wide sets means it says too little.
steps.title: Coverage and width

lessons.summary: The ranked probability score rewards putting probability near the true band. Coverage checks whether the 90 % sets hold 90 % of the time. Width keeps coverage honest.
lessons.title: Scoring probabilities, not just guesses

steps.body:
1. **18 October:** the model, the priors, the band edges, the level thresholds and the coverage tolerance are frozen. The frozen file carries a hash; every prediction row carries that hash.
2. **20–31 October:** the researcher counts the library several times a day, the whole library with the open area and the silent room recorded separately. Counts are sealed through the IP-162 sweeps. Some sweeps are counted by two people, which measures how much counters disagree.
3. **After the last date:** the counts are opened and scored.

The counter does not look at the live occupancy display while counting.
implies: Manual counts never enter the model. They only score it.
steps.title: Freeze, then count

steps.body:
Minutes and sweeps within a day are not independent, so the date is the unit. With 12 dates and about 4 sweeps per date (48 sweeps), and an assumed correlation of 0.3 between sweeps of one date, the 95 % half-widths are roughly:

- level accuracy near 0.7: ±0.13 if sweeps were independent, ±0.18 grouped by date;
- 90 % coverage: ±0.08 if sweeps were independent, ±0.12 grouped by date.

If the fused model beats the calendar on all 12 dates, a sign test gives $p\approx0.0005$. The coverage check can tell 0.70 from 0.90, not 0.86 from 0.90.

check.answer: Under "no difference" each date is a coin flip. Twelve heads in a row has probability $2\times0.5^{12}\approx0.0005$ (two-sided). A mixed record like 8 of 12 would not be convincing.
check.question: Why is a 12-out-of-12 win so convincing when 12 dates is a small sample?

implies: Enough for a one-site result. Not enough for any claim across sites.

symbols.meaning: assumed correlation between sweeps of one date (0.3)

steps.title: How precise can twelve dates be?

steps.body:
- **H2 passes:** the fused levels beat the calendar and each single sensor on the counted dates. A label-free fusion of CSI and Bluetooth reads occupancy levels in a real public building.
- **H3 passes:** the 90 % band sets hold about 90 % of the time under a declared scale prior. Outside scale information is enough for honest count bands.
- **H3 fails, H2 passes:** levels work, but the device scale is wrong or too narrow. The thesis reports which prior failed and how far.
- **Both fail:** empty versus occupied (no scale needed), the characterised instrument (H1) and the released corpus remain as the contribution.
implies: Every outcome is reported per date, with the failures as well as the successes.
steps.title: What each outcome would mean

lessons.summary: Freeze first, count later, open the counts only after the freeze. The date is the independent unit, and twelve dates set the precision.
lessons.thesis: The Library Corpus and Verification Protocol; Blind Evaluation
lessons.title: The blind test

modules.subtitle: Levels, bands, honest confidence, and how 12 counted days decide H2 and H3
modules.title: Outputs and the blind test

steps.body: Every result comes from one building, one hardware family and about two weeks of counted dates. A different room changes the paths, the furniture and the people's devices. Transfer to a second site is future work, not a claim.
implies: The thesis says "in this library, in October 2026", and means it.
steps.title: One library, a few weeks

steps.body: Devices per person is the weakest link (Module 3). The thesis declares two priors from outside facts and lets the blind counts judge them. If both fail, the honest result is "the outside information available is not enough for count bands in persons", together with how far off it was.
implies: A missing published device-per-person ratio is itself a finding.
steps.title: The scale is declared, not measured

steps.body: "Empty" means closed hours and a Bluetooth count at its night floor. A person without an advertising device would pass that rule. The instrument floor and the zero of the count rest on it, so the thesis states it as a rule and reports how often closed minutes fail the Bluetooth check.
steps.title: Certified empty is a rule, not a proof

steps.body: All model choices before the freeze used how well the model predicted the next Bluetooth count. That favours tracking devices. Whether tracking devices well also means tracking people well is exactly what the counts test; the thesis never treats one as the other.
steps.title: The model was selected on devices, not people

lessons.summary: One site, a few weeks, a declared scale, a declared rule for "empty", and selection on device tracking. Each limit has a place in the argument.
lessons.title: The limits that shape every claim

steps.body: The filter of Module 3 multiplies one likelihood per witness. Adding a sensor means writing down how its reading depends on the count, then multiplying one more factor. No retraining of the others is needed.
implies: A sensor that carries its own person scale would narrow the bands directly.

symbols.meaning: the reading of sensor $s$ in the next minute

steps.title: A new sensor is a new likelihood factor

steps.body:
- **CO₂:** slow, but a mass balance links its rise to the number of people breathing, which gives its own person scale.
- **mmWave radar:** counts people, including still ones, in its field of view.
- **Wi-Fi round-trip time and UWB:** fine timing; responds to bodies along the path.
- **Bluetooth signal deformation:** uses Bluetooth as a device-free channel, like CSI.
- **Audio and video:** strong evidence with a high privacy cost.

None of these was deployed in this thesis.
implies: Privacy cost belongs in the choice, next to accuracy and price.
steps.title: Candidate sensors

steps.body: A second site would test transfer. Spatial density (where people sit, not only how many) would need a separate ground truth. Choosing which measurement to take next at a fixed radio budget is a parked direction that this estimator makes possible to test.
steps.title: Further research

lessons.summary: Any sensor with a model of how it responds to the count can join the filter as one more likelihood factor. Each brings its own scale, delay and privacy cost.
lessons.title: Other sensors as more witnesses
